extracted.intended_audience: school and college administrators, Title IX coordinators, campus legal counsel, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements for recipient (K-12 and postsecondary) Title IX grievance processes, focusing on notice, evidence exchange, investigative reports, privacy protections, advisors, and related due-process protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance notice of interviews/meetings/hearings (§106.45(b)(5)(v))
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide to a party notice when that party's participation is invited or expected with respect to any meeting, interview, or hearing during the grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice must be given to the party whose participation is invited or expected (changed language from “the” to “a” to clarify intent). The Department views this as a due-process protection that benefits both complainants and respondents by giving both parties time to prepare and meaningfully participate. Recipients should ensure such notice is provided equally to both parties and should not use this provision to copy advisors indiscriminately; recipients retain discretion to decide whether to copy advisors so long as practices are applied equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial written notice must state whether false statements are prohibited (§106.45(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial written notice to the parties must include a statement about whether the recipient's code of conduct prohibits false statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This informs parties that making false statements (e.g., fabricating an alibi) may be subject to disciplinary consequences; it also helps ensure investigators and decision-makers can take false statements or destruction of evidence into account when assessing credibility and weight of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal opportunity to inspect and review evidence directly related to the allegations (§106.45(b)(5)(vi))
rubrics_metrics.description: Both parties must be given equal opportunity to inspect and review all evidence gathered by the recipient that is directly related to the allegations, including inculpatory and exculpatory evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes transparent disclosure of the universe of relevant and potentially relevant evidence so both parties can prepare arguments, identify overlooked evidence, and contest relevance; includes evidence gathered from law enforcement when applicable. Investigators should not unilaterally screen out or withhold evidence directly related to the allegations; parties may argue about relevance to the investigative report and to the decision-maker. Recipients may redact information that is not directly related, privileged, or otherwise barred from use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten-day review-and-comment period for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should be allowed a period (the final regulations provide a ten-day review and comment period) to read and provide written responses to the evidence gathered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters debated calendar vs. business days, shorter or flexible timelines, and K-12 applicability; Department retained a ten-day period while acknowledging implementation concerns. Recipients should interpret and implement the ten-day period consistent with the regulation and consider institution-specific constraints while ensuring parties have meaningful time to prepare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence exchange format: electronic or hard copy; no mandatory file-share restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must send the evidence subject to inspection and review to each party and the party's advisor (if any), in electronic format or hard copy; recipients are neither required nor prohibited from using a file-sharing platform that restricts downloading or copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may adopt platforms that restrict downloading, but may also provide hard copies. Recipients may require parties/advisors to refrain from disseminating evidence (for example, through a non-disclosure agreement) so long as such practices comply with the regulations and applicable law. Consider accessibility and equity issues (e.g., private computer access, students with disabilities) and privacy risks (photographing screens). Recipients may adopt supervised viewing or hard-copy review practices where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative report must summarize only relevant evidence (§106.45(b)(5)(vii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigative report is required to summarize only “relevant” evidence; evidence summarized in the investigative report must be relevant to the allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department distinguishes between evidence that is “directly related to the allegations” (broader) and evidence that is “relevant” (narrower for the investigative report). The investigator may decide which directly related evidence is relevant to include in the report, but parties can contest those determinations in their responses and at hearings. Crafting a full report before sharing evidence raised concerns among commenters; the Department balances transparency with fairness by permitting parties to review evidence and respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of treatment records — voluntary written consent required (§106.45(b)(5)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient cannot access, consider, disclose, or otherwise use a party's treatment records (records made or maintained by a physician, psychiatrist, psychologist, or other recognized professional/paraprofessional acting in that capacity) unless the recipient obtains the party's voluntary, written consent for use in a grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the party is not an eligible student under FERPA, the recipient must obtain the parent’s voluntary, written consent. This protection applies even if the recipient already has possession of such records. Non-treatment records (financial, sexual history, etc.) may be reviewed only if directly related to the allegations and, for sexual history, only within the narrow exceptions of §106.45(b)(6)(i)-(ii). Recipients should obtain written consent before using treatment records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of sexual predisposition and narrow exceptions for prior sexual behavior (§106.45(b)(6)(i)-(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence about a complainant's sexual predisposition is not relevant and must not be included in the investigative report; evidence about a complainant's prior sexual behavior is not relevant except in the two narrow statutory exceptions enumerated in the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigative report must avoid including sexual predisposition and must include prior sexual behavior only when it fits the narrow exceptions specified. Recipients should apply these exclusions consistently to protect privacy and comply with the regulation's limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redaction and privilege safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may redact information that is not directly related to the allegations or that is otherwise barred from use under §106.45 (e.g., legally recognized privileges, or treatment records without written consent) before sending evidence to parties for inspection and review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redacting confidential information is distinct from withholding evidence that is directly related to the allegations; confidential or sensitive information may still be directly related and therefore subject to review unless specifically barred. Recipients must balance privacy protections with due-process obligations to disclose evidence directly related to allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may impose non-disclosure agreements or restrictions on dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may require parties and advisors to sign non-disclosure agreements or impose restrictions prohibiting dissemination or use of evidence outside the Title IX process, provided doing so does not violate the regulations or other applicable laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such measures can be used to protect privacy/confidentiality, but recipients must ensure these restrictions comply with the regulations and relevant state/federal law (e.g., open-records or rape-shield statutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient discretion to limit advisor participation (§106.45(b)(5)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients retain discretion under §106.45(b)(5)(iv) to limit the participation of party advisors; recipients are not required to copy advisors on all correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to impose a rule requiring copying advisors on all correspondence so as to preserve recipient discretion and each party's choice about advisor involvement. However, nothing prevents a recipient from adopting a practice of copying advisors on notices so long as the practice is applied equally to both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties’ right to select an advisor of choice and access supportive measures (§106.45(b)(5)(iii), §106.44(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties have the right to select an advisor of choice to advise and accompany them throughout the grievance process, and recipients must offer supportive measures to complainants with or without a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures must be offered via an interactive process that takes into account the complainant's wishes and must be available regardless of whether a formal grievance is filed. Advisors may assist parties in reviewing evidence and preparing responses; recipients should facilitate meaningful participation consistent with other provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on retaliation and coercion (§106.71)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.71 prohibits retaliation (including coercion of witnesses) against any person for participating or refusing to participate in a Title IX proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection aims to prevent coercion, witness tampering, or retaliation directed at complainants, respondents, or witnesses. Recipients must enforce anti-retaliation protections and consider them in adjudication and remedial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance due process and victim-centered concerns; impartiality of Title IX personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance process must be designed to promote accuracy through meaningful participation of both parties and to be overseen by impartial, unbiased Title IX personnel who do not prejudge facts and who objectively evaluate inculpatory and exculpatory evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department frames advance notice, equal evidence access, and procedural safeguards as promoting fairness, legitimacy, and truth-seeking. The rules aim to balance due-process protections with sensitivity to trauma and the needs of complainants, including offering supportive measures and preserving complainant autonomy regarding filing formal complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: evidence 'directly related' vs investigator relevance determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence sent to the parties for inspection and review should include all evidence that is “directly related to the allegations,” even if the investigator initially deems some of that evidence irrelevant; parties can then argue about relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to define “directly related” or “relevant,” leaving those terms to plain-meaning interpretation (noting alignment with FERPA). The purpose is to avoid investigators unilaterally screening out potentially disputable evidence and to give parties the opportunity to contest relevance to the decision-maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for K-12 recipients and small institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department recognizes commenters’ concerns that certain provisions (e.g., ten-day review, evidence exchange) may be more burdensome or inappropriate in K-12 settings or for small institutions with limited staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the final regulations apply across recipients, the Department notes that K-12 contexts raise special concerns (shared classrooms, close proximity of parties, restorative justice options) and that small institutions may face resource constraints. Recipients should implement procedures mindful of context while complying with the regulatory requirements; the Department did not exempt K-12 institutions from these obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties entitled to contest omissions or destruction of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party identifies missing evidence or demonstrates that relevant evidence was destroyed by another party, the decision-maker may take that into account in assessing credibility and weight of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations require that parties have the opportunity to inspect and identify missing or destroyed evidence; investigators and decision-makers should consider such findings when evaluating credibility and making responsibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must promote reporting and protect complainant autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must respond promptly and supportively to every complainant when notified of alleged sexual harassment, promote respect for complainant autonomy over whether to initiate a formal grievance process, and protect complainants from retaliation for refusing to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes to §§106.8, 106.30, 106.44, and addition of §106.71 emphasize clear reporting options, offering supportive measures regardless of filing a formal complaint, and preserving complainant choices about initiating grievances. The aim is to assure complainants they can report and receive support without being forced into a grievance process.
